title: Environmental variation and extra-pair paternity in birds
text:
0.1 Analytical strategy
Thisdocuments a reproducible comparative analysis of environmental variation and extra-pair paternity (EPP) in birds. The analysis uses population-level estimates of the proportion of sampled broods containing at least one extra-pair young.
The main analysis is organised around three full environmental model groups. These models test whether broad environmental-geographic gradients, short-term climate anomalies, and long-term climate anomalies are associated with population-level EPP. Each group is fitted as a mean-only beta-binomial mixed model and as a mean-scale model, with methodological controls included in the model set.
The environmental PCA summarises six environmental and geographic variables. The two primary axes are interpreted as PC1, a thermal-geographic gradient, and PC2, a wet-productivity gradient.

title: Environmental variation and extra-pair paternity in birds
text:
0.2 Model roadmap
The main environmental models chapter presents the three primary hypothesis groups: an environmental PCA model, a short-anomaly model, and a long-anomaly model. Each group is fitted with and without a scale component.
The scale component asks whether environmental predictors and methodological controls are associated not only with mean EPP, but also with residual precision and overdispersion in EPP.
The sensitivity models chapter uses environmental-geographic predictors directly, rather than PCA axes or anomaly-only models

title: Environmental variation and extra-pair paternity in birds
text:
0.3 Reproducibility
The workflow first documents data preparation and phylogenetic matching, then describes the common model structure, constructs the environmental PCA, fits the full environmental models, evaluates the scale component, and presents sensitivity analyses and figures.

title: 5  Overall model structure
text:
5.1 Overview
This chapter defines the common statistical structure used across the Bayesian models. It describes the beta-binomial response model, the population, species, and phylogenetic grouping terms used for the expected EPP probability, and the distinction between mean-only and location-scale models. Reference identity (id_reference) is not included as a separate grouping term in the model because the reference-population overlap check in the data-preparation chapter showed that population identity captures the repeated-observation structure used in the main environmental models.

title: 5  Overall model structure
text:
5.2 Response model
For record \(i\), the response is the number of sampled broods with EPP:
\[y_i = \texttt{n\_epp\_broods}_i,\]
out of the total number of sampled broods:
\[n_i = \texttt{n\_broods\_sampled}_i.\]
The model likelihood is:
\[y_i \sim \operatorname{BetaBinomial}(n_i, \mu_i, \phi_i),\]
where \(\mu_i\) is the expected EPP probability and \(\phi_i\) is the beta-binomial precision parameter.

title: 5  Overall model structure
text:
5.3 Expected EPP and grouping structure
The baseline component for the expected EPP probability is:
\[\operatorname{logit}(\mu_i) =
\alpha +
\mathbf{x}_i \boldsymbol{\beta} +
u_{\operatorname{population}[i]} +
v_{\operatorname{species}[i]} +
w_{\operatorname{phylogeny}[i]}.\]
The grouping terms correspond to population identity, non-phylogenetic species identity, and phylogenetic species covariance:
\[u_{\operatorname{population}[i]} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2_{\operatorname{population}}),\]
\[v_{\operatorname{species}[i]} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2_{\operatorname{species}}),\]
\[w_{\operatorname{phylogeny}} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2_{\operatorname{phylogeny}}\mathbf{A}),\]
where \(\mathbf{A}\) is the phylogenetic correlation matrix.
Here \(\mathbf{x}_i \boldsymbol{\beta}\) denotes the fixed-effect part of the model. The exact predictors differ between the environmental models, but the linear predictor always combines fixed effects with the same random-effect structure: population_id, species_nonphylo, and species_phylo with the phylogenetic covariance matrix.
In brms notation, this is:
(1 | population_id) +
(1 | species_nonphylo) +
(1 | gr(species_phylo, cov = phylo_mat))

title: 5  Overall model structure
text:
5.4 Precision parameter
The parameter \(\phi_i\) is the beta-binomial precision parameter. It controls the amount of residual variation around the expected EPP probability \(\mu_i\). Lower precision corresponds to stronger extra-binomial variation among records with the same expected EPP probability. Positive coefficients in the precision component indicate higher precision and lower residual overdispersion; negative coefficients indicate lower precision and higher residual overdispersion.
In mean-only models, the precision parameter is constant across records:
\[\log(\phi_i) = \gamma_0.\]
In mean-scale models, selected predictors are also included in the precision component:
\[\log(\phi_i) =
\gamma_0 +
\mathbf{z}_i \boldsymbol{\gamma}.\]
Here \(\mathbf{z}_i \boldsymbol{\gamma}\) denotes the fixed-effect part of the scale model. Thus, mean-only models ask whether predictors explain average EPP, whereas mean-scale models additionally ask whether predictors explain variation in the precision of EPP estimates.

title: 5  Overall model structure
text:
5.5 Baseline overall model
The baseline overall model uses only the common grouping structure, without environmental predictors:
\[\operatorname{logit}(\mu_i) =
\alpha +
u_{\operatorname{population}[i]} +
v_{\operatorname{species}[i]} +
w_{\operatorname{phylogeny}[i]}.\]
The precision component is:
\[\log(\phi_i) = \gamma_0.\]
In brms notation:


Show code
m_overall_population <- brms::brm(
  n_epp_broods | trials(n_broods_sampled) ~
    1 +
    (1 | population_id) +
    (1 | species_nonphylo) +
    (1 | gr(species_phylo, cov = phylo_mat_fit)),
  data = dat_model,
  data2 = list(phylo_mat_fit = phylo_mat_fit),
  family = brms::beta_binomial(link = "logit", link_phi = "log")
)

6.1 Overview
The environmental predictors combine climate, productivity, and geography. These variables describe related ecological gradients and should not be interpreted as fully independent axes of variation. We therefore use principal component analysis (PCA) to construct a small number of orthogonal predictors for the main environmental models.
The PCA is fitted to complete cases for the selected environmental-geographic variables.

title: 6  PCA for environmental predictors
text:
6.7 Interpretation
Based on the loadings, PC1 was interpreted as a thermal-geographic gradient. In this dataset, higher PC1 values correspond to warmer sites with greater diurnal temperature range, lower absolute latitude, and greater distance from the coast.
Based on the loadings, PC2 was interpreted as a wet-productivity gradient after orienting the axis. In this dataset, higher PC2 values correspond to wetter sites with higher NDVI.
These two axes are used as the main environmental predictors in the beta-binomial EPP models.

title: 7  Main environmental models
text:
7.1 Overview
This chapter defines the final primary environmental model set. The primary model set was organised around three environmental hypotheses.
Each hypothesis group was fitted as a mean-only model and as a location-scale model, allowing environmental predictors to affect the expected EPP rate and, in the mean-scale version, allowing environmental predictors and methodological controls to affect residual dispersion. Methodological controls are nest_box and marker_type. All models use the same random-effect structure for population, non-phylogenetic species identity, and phylogenetic species covariance.

title: 7  Main environmental models
text:
The PCA models tested whether broad environmental-geographic gradients were associated with EPP.
The short-anomaly models tested whether recent deviations from local climatic conditions were associated with EPP.
The long-anomaly models tested whether deviations from the 1961-1989 climatic baseline were associated with EPP.

title: 8  Sensitivity models
text:
8.1 Overview
This chapter defines the sensitivity analysis for the direct environmental predictor set. The same fixed effects are fitted in two versions: a mean-only model with a single global precision parameter (phi ~ 1) and a location- scale model where the environmental-geographic predictors and methodological controls are also included in the scale component.
Both models include methodological controls (nest_box, marker_type) and the same population, species, and phylogenetic random-effect structure as the main models.

9.2 Phylogenetic Distribution of High-EPP Species
This figure shows the phylogenetic distribution of species with the highest observed species-level EPP rates. Highlighted tips represent the species with the highest aggregate EPP estimates among species included in the pruned phylogeny. The figure is descriptive and is used to illustrate that high EPP values are distributed across the avian phylogeny rather than being restricted to a single narrow clade.


Show code
tree_file <- "data/processed/tree_pruned.rds"
dat_phylo_file <- "data/processed/dat_model_phylo.rds"

if (file.exists(tree_file) &&
    file.exists(dat_phylo_file) &&
    requireNamespace("ape", quietly = TRUE)) {
  tree_pruned <- readRDS(tree_file)
  dat_phylo <- readRDS(dat_phylo_file)

  high_epp_species <- dat_phylo %>%
    filter(
      !is.na(species_phylo),
      !is.na(n_epp_broods),
      !is.na(n_broods_sampled),
      n_broods_sampled > 0
    ) %>%
    group_by(species_phylo) %>%
    summarise(
      n_records = n(),
      total_broods = sum(n_broods_sampled),
      total_epp_broods = sum(n_epp_broods),
      species_epp_rate = total_epp_broods / total_broods,
      .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%
    filter(species_phylo %in% tree_pruned$tip.label) %>%
    arrange(desc(species_epp_rate), desc(total_broods)) %>%
    slice_head(n = 10)

  write_csv(
    high_epp_species,
    "figures/high_epp_species_for_phylogeny.csv"
  )

  top_species <- high_epp_species$species_phylo
  tip_colours <- ifelse(tree_pruned$tip.label %in% top_species, "#b35c35", "grey55")

  make_phylogeny_plot <- function() {
    ape::plot.phylo(
      tree_pruned,
      type = "fan",
      show.tip.label = FALSE,
      edge.color = "grey70",
      edge.width = 0.7,
      no.margin = TRUE
    )

    ape::tiplabels(
      pch = 21,
      bg = tip_colours,
      col = "white",
      cex = ifelse(tree_pruned$tip.label %in% top_species, 1.1, 0.45),
      lwd = 0.25
    )

    legend(
      "topleft",
      legend = c("Top species-level EPP", "Other species"),
      pt.bg = c("#b35c35", "grey55"),
      pch = 21,
      pt.cex = c(1.1, 0.7),
      bty = "n",
      cex = 0.85
    )

    legend(
      "bottomleft",
      legend = gsub("_", " ", top_species),
      pch = 21,
      pt.bg = "#b35c35",
      bty = "n",
      cex = 0.55,
      title = "Highest EPP species"
    )
  }

  png("figures/high_epp_species_phylogeny.png", width = 2400, height = 2400, res = 300)
  make_phylogeny_plot()
  dev.off()

  pdf("figures/high_epp_species_phylogeny.pdf", width = 8, height = 8)
  make_phylogeny_plot()
  dev.off()
} else {
  cat("Phylogenetic tree, model-ready data, or the ape package is not available yet.")
}

main_fixed_effects_file <- file.path(

9.6 Sensitivity Environmental Effects
This figure shows model-predicted EPP along the four direct environmental predictors from the mean-only sensitivity model. The fitted lines represent posterior mean predictions and shaded intervals show 95% credible intervals. Raw population-level EPP values are shown lightly in the background only to indicate the distribution of observations across each predictor.


Show code
sensitivity_mu_model_file <- file.path(
  "models/sensitivity_models",
  "m_sensitivity_first_month_mu.rds"
)

sensitivity_data_file <- first_existing(c(
  file.path("models/sensitivity_models", "dat_sensitivity_models.rds"),
  file.path("models/sensitivity_models", "dat_fit_sensitivity_models.rds")
))

if (file.exists(sensitivity_mu_model_file) &&
    !is.na(sensitivity_data_file) &&
    requireNamespace("brms", quietly = TRUE)) {
  sensitivity_mu_model <- readRDS(sensitivity_mu_model_file)
  dat_sensitivity_effects <- readRDS(sensitivity_data_file) %>%
    mutate(
      observed_epp = n_epp_broods / n_broods_sampled,
      nest_box = factor(nest_box),
      marker_type = factor(marker_type)
    )

  sensitivity_effect_variables <- tribble(
    ~variable, ~label,
    "tmp_cru_C_first_month_z", "Temperature",
    "pre_cru_mm_first_month_log_z", "Precipitation",
    "dtr_cru_C_first_month_z", "DTR",
    "ndvi_first_month_median_30km_z", "NDVI"
  )

  make_sensitivity_effect <- function(variable, label) {
    x_range <- range(dat_sensitivity_effects[[variable]], na.rm = TRUE)
    x_grid <- seq(x_range[1], x_range[2], length.out = 80)

    newdata <- dat_sensitivity_effects[rep(1, length(x_grid)), , drop = FALSE]
    newdata$tmp_cru_C_first_month_z <- 0
    newdata$pre_cru_mm_first_month_log_z <- 0
    newdata$dtr_cru_C_first_month_z <- 0
    newdata$ndvi_first_month_median_30km_z <- 0
    newdata$abs_latitude_z <- 0
    newdata$distance_to_coast_z <- 0
    newdata$nest_box <- factor(levels(dat_sensitivity_effects$nest_box)[1], levels = levels(dat_sensitivity_effects$nest_box))
    newdata$marker_type <- factor(levels(dat_sensitivity_effects$marker_type)[1], levels = levels(dat_sensitivity_effects$marker_type))
    newdata$n_broods_sampled <- 1
    newdata[[variable]] <- x_grid

    fitted_values <- fitted(
      sensitivity_mu_model,
      newdata = newdata,
      re_formula = NA,
      scale = "response"
    )

    tibble(
      variable = label,
      x = x_grid,
      estimate = fitted_values[, "Estimate"],
      lower = fitted_values[, "Q2.5"],
      upper = fitted_values[, "Q97.5"]
    )
  }

  sensitivity_effect_plot_data <- pmap_dfr(
    sensitivity_effect_variables,
    make_sensitivity_effect
  )

  sensitivity_effect_raw_data <- pmap_dfr(
    sensitivity_effect_variables,
    function(variable, label) {
      dat_sensitivity_effects %>%
        transmute(
          variable = label,
          x = .data[[variable]],
          observed_epp = observed_epp
        ) %>%
        drop_na()
    }
  )

  sensitivity_effect_levels <- sensitivity_effect_variables$label

  fig_sensitivity_environmental_effects <- ggplot() +
    geom_point(
      data = sensitivity_effect_raw_data,
      aes(x = x, y = observed_epp),
      alpha = 0.12,
      size = 0.8,
      colour = "grey35"
    ) +
    geom_ribbon(
      data = sensitivity_effect_plot_data,
      aes(x = x, ymin = lower, ymax = upper),
      fill = "#9fb9bd",
      alpha = 0.35
    ) +
    geom_line(
      data = sensitivity_effect_plot_data,
      aes(x = x, y = estimate),
      colour = "#b35c35",
      linewidth = 0.8
    ) +
    facet_wrap(
      ~ factor(variable, levels = sensitivity_effect_levels),
      scales = "free_x",
      ncol = 2
    ) +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1), limits = c(0, 1)) +
    labs(
      x = "Standardised predictor value",
      y = "Predicted EPP"
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      strip.text = element_text(colour = "grey25")
    )

  ggsave(
    "figures/sensitivity_environmental_effects.png",
    fig_sensitivity_environmental_effects,
    width = 8.5,
    height = 5.8,
    dpi = 300
  )

  ggsave(
    "figures/sensitivity_environmental_effects.pdf",
    fig_sensitivity_environmental_effects,
    width = 8.5,
    height = 5.8
  )
} else {
  cat("Sensitivity mean-only model or data are not available yet.")

  sensitivity_mu_model <- readRDS(sensitivity_mu_model_file)
  sensitivity_draws <- posterior::as_draws_df(sensitivity_mu_model)
  available_terms <- intersect(names(sensitivity_fixed_effect_terms), names(sensitivity_draws))

  sensitivity_fixed_effects <- map_dfr(available_terms, function(term) {
    x <- sensitivity_draws[[term]]
    tibble(
      model = "Mean-only sensitivity",
      term = term,
      predictor = sensitivity_fixed_effect_terms[[term]],
      component = "mu",
      estimate = median(x),
      lower = quantile(x, 0.025),
      upper = quantile(x, 0.975),
      prob_positive = mean(x > 0),
      prob_negative = mean(x < 0)
    )
  })

  write_csv(
    sensitivity_fixed_effects,
    file.path(sensitivity_model_dir, "fixed_effects_sensitivity_models.csv")
  )

  term_order <- names(sensitivity_fixed_effect_terms)[
    names(sensitivity_fixed_effect_terms) %in% available_terms
  ]

  sensitivity_draws_matrix <- as.matrix(sensitivity_draws[, term_order, drop = FALSE])

  fig_sensitivity_fixed_effects <- bayesplot::mcmc_intervals(
    sensitivity_draws_matrix,
    pars = term_order,
    prob = 0.8,
    prob_outer = 0.95,
    point_est = "median",
    outer_size = 0.7,
    inner_size = 1.8,
    point_size = 2.4
  ) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.4, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey45") +
    scale_y_discrete(
      limits = rev(term_order),
      labels = sensitivity_fixed_effect_terms
    ) +
    labs(
      title = "First-month mean-only",
      x = NULL,
      y = NULL
    ) +
    bayesplot::theme_default(base_size = 11) +
    theme(
      plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, colour = "grey25", face = "plain"),
      axis.text.y = element_text(colour = "grey25"),
      axis.text.x = element_text(colour = "grey25"),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major.y = element_line(colour = "grey90"),
      panel.grid.major.x = element_line(colour = "grey90")
    )

  ggsave(
    "figures/sensitivity_fixed_effects_forest_plot.png",
    fig_sensitivity_fixed_effects,
    width = 9,
    height = 3.2,
    dpi = 300
  )

  ggsave(
    "figures/sensitivity_fixed_effects_forest_plot.pdf",
    fig_sensitivity_fixed_effects,
    width = 9,
    height = 3.2
  )
} else {
  cat("Sensitivity fixed-effect figure will be generated after the model object and bayesplot are available.")
}
